observation.visible_scene: A person's two hands hold a large spherical object built from many small polished silver magnetic spheres and square magnetic tiles arranged in patchwork clusters, against a plain light-gray background. The sphere has a dark opening/hole near its center that reveals an interior lattice. The hands grip the sphere at its left and right sides throughout the excerpt.
visible_changes: The sphere is continuously and slowly rotated/tumbled in the hands, so different patterned faces pass across the frame; this is object rotation, not a camera pan (the plain background and hand entry points stay essentially fixed).

A bright, highly reflective 2x2 tile cluster shifts position across the surface from frame to frame (e.g., right-of-center early, then moving toward the left and back toward the right later), confirming the sphere's turning.

The apparent size and visibility of the central hole change with the viewing angle: it looks like a small depression early on, opens into a clear see-through gap through the middle frames, and remains partly visible at the end, consistent with rotation rather than the structure expanding or collapsing.
The hands make small grip adjustments as they turn the sphere; the right hand's thumb and fingers reposition slightly over time, and the left hand's contact shifts a little lower in later frames.
Specular highlights on the tiles and balls move across the surface as the orientation changes, but no tiles or balls detach or are added within the segment.
outside_clip_unknowns: How the sphere was assembled and whether the central hole is a permanent feature of this build.
What the person does with the sphere before this crop begins or after it ends.
The full extent of the rotation (whether it completes a full turn).
uncertain_details: Whether there is any slight camera movement is hard to judge because the background is featureless; the dominant motion is the sphere's rotation.
The exact axis of rotation is not directly measurable from the samples.
The bright reflective patches could be tile clusters catching light rather than distinct colored pieces.
